questions.q: List the items of food available to people in Harappan cities. Identify the groups who would have provided these.
answer: The Harappans consumed a wide range of plant and animal products, including fish. Archaeologists reconstruct this diet from charred grains and seeds, studied by archaeo-botanists, and from animal bones, studied by archaeo-zoologists.

answer.text: wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame are found at Harappan sites. Millets appear at sites in Gujarat, while finds of rice are relatively rare.
bones of cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig indicate that these domesticated animals were eaten. Bones of wild species such as boar, deer and gharial, as well as of fish and fowl, are also found.

farmers supplied grain — the bull is represented on seals and terracotta sculpture, terracotta plough models come from Cholistan and Banawali, and a ploughed field with two sets of furrows at right angles was found at Kalibangan. Pastoralists supplied milk and meat from domesticated herds. Fisherfolk supplied fish and fowl. For wild game we cannot be certain: the chapter states that we do not know whether the Harappans hunted these animals themselves or obtained meat from other hunting communities.

questions.q: How do archaeologists trace socio-economic differences in Harappan society? What are the differences that they notice?
answer: Archaeologists use two principal strategies — the study of burials and the study of artefacts.

answer.text: At Harappan sites the dead were generally laid in pits. Sometimes the burial pit differed in the way it was made; in some instances the hollowed-out spaces were lined with bricks. Whether such variations indicate social differences remains uncertain. Some graves contain pottery and ornaments, perhaps reflecting a belief that these could be used in the afterlife. Jewellery occurs in burials of both men and women. In the mid-1980s excavations at the cemetery in Harappa, an ornament of three shell rings, a jasper bead and hundreds of micro beads was found near the skull of a male. Copper mirrors accompany some burials. On the whole, however, the Harappans did not bury precious things with the dead.

These are broadly classified as utilitarian — querns, pottery, needles, flesh-rubbers of ordinary stone or clay, distributed throughout settlements — and luxuries, which are rare, made of costly non-local materials or by complicated technologies, such as little pots of faience.

Rare objects of valuable material concentrate in large settlements such as Mohenjodaro and Harappa and are rare in smaller ones; miniature faience pots, possibly perfume bottles, are absent from Kalibangan. Gold was rare and precious, and all gold jewellery found at Harappan sites came from hoards. Yet ambiguity persists — spindle whorls of faience are difficult to classify — and the chapter notes as an open problem why Harappan cemeteries show so little social differentiation.

questions.q: Would you agree that the drainage system in Harappan cities indicates town planning? Give reasons for your answer.
answer: Yes. The carefully planned drainage system is described as one of the most distinctive features of Harappan cities, and it points unmistakably to planning.

answer.text: In the plan of the Lower Town, roads and streets were laid out along an approximate "grid" pattern, intersecting at right angles. It appears that streets with drains were laid out first and houses built along them afterwards. Since domestic waste water had to flow into the street drains, every house needed at least one wall along a street — a requirement that could only be met if drainage was designed before construction.

Every house had a brick-paved bathroom with drains connected through the wall to the street drains. House drains first emptied into a sump or cesspit in which solid matter settled while waste water flowed out into the street drains. Main channels were made of bricks set in mortar and covered with loose bricks that could be removed for cleaning; limestone was sometimes used for covers. Very long channels were provided at intervals with sumps for cleaning. Mackay described it as the most complete ancient system then discovered.
Drainage was found in smaller settlements too: at Lothal, houses were of mud brick while drains were built of burnt bricks.

answer: Taken with the mud brick platforms, the fixed building area and the standardised brick ratio, the drains confirm that the settlement was first planned and then implemented accordingly.

questions.q: List the materials used to make beads in the Harappan civilisation. Describe the process by which any one kind of bead was made.

answer.text: The variety is remarkable — stones such as carnelian (of a beautiful red colour), jasper, crystal, quartz and steatite; metals such as copper, bronze and gold; and shell, faience and terracotta or burnt clay. Some beads were made of two or more stones cemented together, and some of stone with gold caps. Shapes were numerous: disc-shaped, cylindrical, spherical, barrel-shaped and segmented. Some were decorated by incising or painting, and some had designs etched onto them.

Archaeologists' experiments have revealed that the red colour of carnelian was obtained by firing the yellowish raw material and the beads at various stages of production. Nodules were first chipped into rough shapes and then finely flaked into the final form. Grinding, polishing and drilling completed the process. Specialised drills for this purpose have been found at Chanhudaro, Lothal and, more recently, at Dholavira.

Steatite, a very soft stone, was easily worked. Some beads were moulded out of a paste made with steatite powder, which permitted a variety of shapes unlike the geometrical forms made out of harder stones. How the steatite micro bead was made remains a puzzle for archaeologists studying ancient technology.

answer: Finished beads from Chanhudaro and Lothal were probably taken to the large urban centres of Mohenjodaro and Harappa.

questions.q: Look at Fig. 1.30 (A Harappan burial) and describe what you see. How is the body placed? What are the objects placed near it? Are there any artefacts on the body? Do these indicate the sex of the skeleton?
answer: The figure shows a complete human skeleton lying within a rectangular pit, consistent with the chapter's statement that at Harappan sites the dead were generally laid in pits.

answer.text: The body lies extended on its back, in a supine position, with the limbs laid straight and the head at one end of the pit.

A group of pottery vessels — including jars, a small pot and dish-on-stand forms — is placed near the head. Such grave goods correspond to the graves that contain pottery and ornaments, perhaps indicating a belief that these could be used in the afterlife.

No conspicuous ornament is visible on the skeleton itself. In other instances the dead were buried with copper mirrors, and at the Harappa cemetery an ornament of three shell rings, a jasper bead and micro beads was found near the skull of a male. On the whole, though, the Harappans did not believe in burying precious things with the dead.

The objects do not indicate the sex. Jewellery has been found in burials of both men and women, so grave goods cannot by themselves determine whether the individual was male or female; that determination must rest on skeletal analysis.

questions.q: Describe some of the distinctive features of Mohenjodaro.
answer: Perhaps the most unique feature of the Harappan civilisation was the development of urban centres, and Mohenjodaro is the best-known of these. Although Harappa was the first site to be discovered, it was badly destroyed by brick robbers — as early as 1875 Alexander Cunningham noted that brick taken from the ancient site was enough to lay about 100 miles of railway line between Lahore and Multan. Mohenjodaro, by contrast, was far better preserved, and at about 125 hectares it was a large city compared with a tiny craft settlement such as Chanhudaro of under 7 hectares.

answer.text: The site is divided into two sections: one smaller but higher, designated the Citadel, and the other much larger but lower, the Lower Town. The Citadel owes its height to buildings constructed on mud brick platforms, and it was walled, which meant that it was physically separated from the Lower Town. The Lower Town was also walled, and several buildings within it were built on platforms serving as foundations.

It has been calculated that if one labourer moved roughly a cubic metre of earth daily, the foundations alone would have required four million person-days — mobilising labour on a very large scale. Once the platforms were in place, all building activity was restricted to a fixed area upon them, so the settlement was first planned and then implemented accordingly. Bricks, whether sun-dried or baked, were of a standardised ratio in which length and breadth were four times and twice the height respectively, a ratio used at all Harappan settlements.

Roads and streets in the Lower Town were laid out along an approximate grid pattern, intersecting at right angles. Streets with drains were laid out first and houses built along them, and since domestic waste water had to flow into the street drains, every house needed at least one wall along a street.

Residential buildings were centred on a courtyard with rooms on all sides; the courtyard was probably the centre of activities such as cooking and weaving, particularly in hot and dry weather. There is an apparent concern for privacy: there are no windows in the walls along the ground level, and the main entrance does not give a direct view of the interior or the courtyard. Every house had its own brick-paved bathroom with drains connected through the wall to the street drains; some houses retain staircases leading to a second storey or the roof; many had wells, often in a room that could be reached from the outside. Scholars estimate the total number of wells in Mohenjodaro at about 700.

These include the warehouse, a massive structure of which only the lower brick portions remain since the upper portions, probably of wood, decayed long ago; and the Great Bath, a large rectangular tank in a courtyard surrounded by a corridor on all four sides, with two flights of steps on the north and south, made watertight by setting bricks on edge and using a mortar of gypsum. Rooms lay on three sides, one containing a large well, and water from the tank flowed into a huge drain. Across a lane to the north stood a smaller building with eight bathrooms, four on each side of a corridor. The uniqueness of the structure and the context in which it was found have led scholars to suggest a special ritual bath.

questions.q: List the raw materials required for craft production in the Harappan civilisation and discuss how these might have been obtained.
answer: Harappan crafts — bead-making, shell-cutting, metal-working, seal-making and weight-making, as practised almost exclusively at Chanhudaro — required a wide range of materials, and the strategies for obtaining them reveal the geographical reach of the civilisation.

answer.text: Stones included carnelian, jasper, crystal, quartz and steatite for beads; steatite for seals; chert for the cubical weights; and lapis lazuli, a blue stone that was apparently very highly valued. Metals included copper, bronze and gold. Other materials were shell, faience — made of ground sand or silica mixed with colour and a gum and then fired — and terracotta or burnt clay. Clay was locally available, but stone, timber and metal had to be procured from outside the alluvial plain.

answer.lead: Strategy one: settlements at the source.
answer.text: The Harappans established settlements in areas where materials occurred. Nageshwar and Balakot, both near the coast, lay where shell was available and became specialised centres for shell objects — bangles, ladles and inlay — which were taken to other settlements. Shortughai in far-off Afghanistan lay near the best source of lapis lazuli. Lothal was near sources of carnelian from Bharuch in Gujarat, steatite from south Rajasthan and north Gujarat, and metal from Rajasthan.

Expeditions may have been sent to the Khetri region of Rajasthan for copper and to south India for gold. These established communication with local communities, and occasional finds of Harappan artefacts such as steatite micro beads in these areas indicate such contact. In the Khetri area archaeologists identify the Ganeshwar–Jodhpura culture, with its distinctive non-Harappan pottery and an unusual wealth of copper objects; its inhabitants possibly supplied copper to the Harappans.

answer.lead: Strategy three: contact with distant lands.
answer.text: Copper was also probably brought from Oman. Chemical analyses show that both Omani copper and Harappan artefacts carry traces of nickel, suggesting a common origin. A distinctive large Harappan jar coated with a thick layer of black clay, such coatings preventing the percolation of liquids, has been found at Omani sites. Mesopotamian texts of the third millennium BCE mention copper from Magan, perhaps a name for Oman. The same texts mention Dilmun, probably Bahrain, and Meluhha, possibly the Harappan region, from which came carnelian, lapis lazuli, copper, gold and varieties of wood. Harappan seals, weights and beads found abroad, the round "Persian Gulf" seal from Bahrain carrying Harappan motifs, and Dilmun weights following the Harappan standard all confirm the exchange.

Terracotta toy models of bullock carts suggest that carts moved goods along land routes. Riverine routes along the Indus and its tributaries and coastal routes were probably used as well; Mesopotamian texts refer to Meluhha as a land of seafarers, and depictions of ships and boats appear on seals.

questions.q: Discuss how archaeologists reconstruct the past.
answer: The Harappan script remains undeciphered, so it is material evidence rather than the written word that allows archaeologists to reconstruct Harappan life — pottery, tools, ornaments, household objects and structures.

answer.text: Organic materials such as cloth, leather, wood and reeds generally decompose, especially in tropical regions; what survives is stone, burnt clay or terracotta, and metal. Moreover, only broken or useless objects would have been thrown away while other things were recycled. Valuable artefacts found intact were therefore either lost in the past or hoarded and never retrieved, which means such finds are accidental rather than typical.

One simple principle of classification is by material — stone, clay, metal, bone, ivory. The second and more complicated is by function: archaeologists must decide whether an object is a tool, an ornament, both, or something meant for ritual use. Function is often inferred from resemblance to present-day things and from the context of discovery — was the object found in a house, a drain, a grave or a kiln? Where direct evidence fails, indirect evidence is used: although traces of cotton occur at some sites, clothing has to be reconstructed from depictions in sculpture.

The first Harappan seal found could not be understood until archaeologists had a context in which to place it — both the cultural sequence in which it was found and a comparison with finds in Mesopotamia.

Archaeo-botanists study ancient plant remains such as charred grains and seeds; archaeo-zoologists study animal bones to establish domestication. Archaeogenetics, the study of the DNA of ancient populations, has been applied at Rakhigarhi in Hisar district, the largest Harappan city at 550 hectares, by Deccan College Deemed University with the Centre for Cellular and Molecular Biology, Hyderabad and Harvard Medical College; the same team reconstructed 3D facial features of Harappan men and women.

Continued occupation builds up occupational debris called a mound. Occupations are detected as layers differing in colour, texture and artefacts, while abandonment produces "sterile layers". Generally the lowest layers are the oldest and the highest the most recent, and the study of these layers — stratigraphy — assigns artefacts to cultural periods. Marshall tended to excavate along regular horizontal units, ignoring stratigraphy, so contextual information was lost; Wheeler, who took over as Director-General in 1944, insisted that excavation follow the stratigraphy of the mound.

Reconstruction is hardest for religion: terracotta female figurines were called mother goddesses, a seated stone statue the "priest-king", and a cross-legged figure on a seal was read as "proto-Shiva" — though Rudra in the Rigveda is neither Pashupati nor a yogi. A careful re-examination of data can reverse earlier conclusions: Wheeler read the Mohenjodaro skeletons as evidence of massacre and invasion, but in the 1960s George Dales showed that the skeletons did not belong to the same period and that there was no destruction level, no burning and no evidence of a final defence.

questions.q: Discuss the functions that may have been performed by rulers in Harappan society.
answer: The chapter approaches this question indirectly, since archaeological records provide no immediate answer when we look for a centre of power or for depictions of people in power. What they do provide are indications of complex decisions being taken and implemented, from which the functions of authority may be inferred.

answer.text: There is an extraordinary uniformity of Harappan artefacts, evident in pottery, seals, weights and bricks. Bricks, though obviously not produced in any single centre, were of a uniform ratio throughout the region from Jammu to Gujarat. Settlements were strategically set up in specific locations. Labour was mobilised for making bricks and for constructing massive walls and platforms — the foundations at Mohenjodaro alone are estimated at four million person-days.

First, planning and enforcing urban layout, since the settlement was first planned and then implemented and streets with drains were laid before houses. Second, standardisation — of the brick ratio and of a precise system of chert weights, cubical, with lower denominations binary (1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32) and higher decimal (160, 200, 320, 640). Third, mobilisation and organisation of large labour forces. Fourth, procurement: establishing settlements such as Nageshwar, Balakot, Shortughai and Lothal near raw material sources and sending expeditions to Khetri and south India. Fifth, regulation of exchange and communication, since seals and sealings authenticated consignments. Sixth, possibly ritual functions, if the Great Bath was meant for a special ritual bath.

Some archaeologists hold that Harappan society had no rulers and that everybody enjoyed equal status. Others feel there was no single ruler but several — a separate ruler for Mohenjodaro, another for Harappa. Yet others argue for a single state, given the similarity in artefacts, the evidence for planned settlements, the standardised ratio of brick size, and the establishment of settlements near sources of raw material — a view many find the most plausible.

A large building at Mohenjodaro was labelled a palace, but no spectacular finds were associated with it. The stone statue continues to be called the "priest-king" only because archaeologists familiar with Mesopotamian priest-kings found parallels in the Indus region. Since the ritual practices of the civilisation are not well understood, there is no means of knowing whether those who performed them also held political power. Any account of Harappan rulership therefore remains an inference from uniformity, planning and mobilisation rather than a description drawn from direct evidence.

questions.q: On an outline map, mark the Harappan sites where evidence of agriculture, of craft production, and of raw materials has been recovered.

answer.text: Kalibangan (Rajasthan), where a ploughed field with two sets of furrows at right angles was found; Banawali (Haryana) and the sites in Cholistan, which yielded terracotta plough models; Dholavira (Gujarat), with its water reservoirs; and Shortughai (Afghanistan), where traces of canals were found. Grain finds of wheat, barley, lentil, chickpea and sesame occur generally at Harappan sites, while millets are reported from Gujarat.

answer.lead: Sites with evidence of craft production.
answer.text: Chanhudaro, a tiny settlement almost exclusively devoted to crafts; Lothal and Dholavira, where specialised drills have been found; Nageshwar and Balakot, specialised centres for shell objects; and Mohenjodaro and Harappa, where minute waste traces show craft was undertaken in the large cities too.

answer.lead: Sites and regions where raw materials were found.
answer.text: Nageshwar and Balakot for shell; Shortughai (Afghanistan) for lapis lazuli; Bharuch (Gujarat) for carnelian; south Rajasthan and north Gujarat for steatite; Rajasthan for metal and the Khetri region for copper; south India for gold; and, beyond the subcontinent, Oman for copper.

Waste is one of the best indicators of craft work: to identify centres of production, archaeologists look for raw material such as stone nodules, whole shells and copper ore; tools; unfinished objects; and rejects and waste material.

questions.q: Prepare a report on ten Harappan items as they would be displayed in a museum, describing how old they are, where they were found, and why they are on display.
answer: The chapter notes that Harappan pottery can be seen in the National Museum, Delhi, or in the site museum at Lothal. The following ten items, all illustrated or described in the chapter, would form a representative display. Their dates fall within the span 6000 BCE–1300 BCE, most belonging to the Mature Harappan urban phase of 2600–1900 BCE.

list: The Harappan seal — made of steatite, bearing animal motifs and an undeciphered script; the object through which the civilisation was recognised (first sketched by Cunningham; similar seals found by Daya Ram Sahni at Harappa and Rakhal Das Banerji at Mohenjodaro led to Marshall's announcement of 1924).
Beads, weights and blades — displayed together as craft, exchange and daily technology; the cubical weights are of chert with no markings.
A terracotta bull — from which archaeologists extrapolate that oxen were used for ploughing.
Copper tools — raising the open question of whether harvesting used stone blades in wooden handles or metal tools.
A saddle quern — found in numbers at Mohenjodaro; the second, pounding type was dubbed the "curry stone" by Mackay's workmen.
A copper mirror — recovered from burials.
A faience pot — faience (ground sand or silica + colour + gum, fired) was precious and difficult to make; miniature pots cluster at Mohenjodaro and Harappa.
Painted pottery — illustrating the extraordinary uniformity of Harappan artefacts (in the National Museum, Delhi, and the Lothal site museum).
A terracotta female figurine — heavily jewelled, regarded by early archaeologists as a mother goddess; shows how interpretation can outrun evidence.
The stone statue called the "priest-king" — seated with one hand on the knee; so named from Mesopotamian parallels.

answer: Other display-worthy objects include the sealing from Ropar, the signboard from Dholavira, the "proto-Shiva" seal, the terracotta cart, the conical stones described as gamesmen or lingas, and the skeletal remains from Rakhigarhi from which DNA was extracted.

questions.q: Compare ten things made of stone, metal and clay produced and used at present with the Harappan objects in this chapter, and discuss the similarities and differences.

answer.text: The chapter itself sanctions this exercise: the function of an artefact is often shaped by its resemblance with present-day things — beads, querns, stone blades and pots are obvious examples. Mackay compared present-day querns with what he found, and his cook asked for the loan of a "curry stone" from the museum, a striking demonstration of functional continuity.

Stone: saddle querns and grinding stones for cereals and spices persist in Indian kitchens. Clay: storage jars, cooking vessels, dishes and lamps of burnt clay continue in use, still decorated by painting and incising. Metal: copper and bronze vessels, tools and mirrors have counterparts today, as do beads and bangles of shell, terracotta and semi-precious stone. Weights and scale-pans still regulate exchange, drains still carry waste water, bullock carts remain in use, and gaming pieces still resemble Mackay's small cones.

Present-day objects are largely industrially produced from glass, steel and plastic, whereas Harappan objects were hand-made from stone, burnt clay, copper, bronze, shell and faience; faience itself is no longer common. Mirrors are now of glass rather than polished copper. Above all, Harappan objects carry an undeciphered script and motifs whose meaning is lost.

Many reconstructions rest on the assumption that later traditions provide parallels with earlier ones, since archaeologists move from the known to the unknown. This is plausible for stone querns and pots, but becomes speculative when extended to "religious" symbols — a caution this comparison must carry throughout.

questions.q: Are there similarities or differences in the distribution of Early and Mature Harappan settlements?
answer: The Mature Harappan culture developed in some of the areas occupied by the Early Harappan cultures, so the two distributions overlap substantially along the Indus and its tributaries, with Amri-Nal, Kot Diji, Damb Sadaat and Siswal marking the earlier occupation. The Mature Harappan distribution is however much wider, extending from Manda in the north to Sutkagendor in the west and to Dholavira, Lothal, Nageshwar and Rangpur in Gujarat. Both phases shared certain common elements, including subsistence strategies.

questions.q: What is the evidence used by archaeologists to reconstruct dietary practices?
answer: Charred grains and seeds recovered from sites, studied by archaeo-botanists; animal bones, including those of fish and fowl, studied by archaeo-zoologists, whose analysis indicates that cattle, sheep, goat, buffalo and pig were domesticated; and the grinding equipment and vessels for mixing, blending and cooking made of stone, metal and terracotta, such as the saddle querns of Mohenjodaro.

questions.q: Could the copper tools shown have been used for harvesting?
answer: The chapter leaves the question open. Archaeologists have tried to identify the tools used for harvesting and ask whether the Harappans used stone blades set in wooden handles or metal tools. Copper tools were certainly in use, but the evidence does not settle which was employed in the fields.

questions.q: Is a present-day analogy (as when Mackay compared present-day querns with what he found) a useful strategy?
answer: It is useful but limited. Function is often inferred from an artefact's resemblance to present-day things, and querns, beads, stone blades and pots are obvious examples where the analogy holds. But archaeologists move from the known to the unknown, from the present to the past, and while this is plausible for querns and pots, it becomes more speculative when extended to "religious" symbols — as with the conical stones read as lingas, which Mackay himself thought might equally be board-game pieces.

questions.q: How is the Lower Town different from the Citadel?
answer: The Citadel is smaller but higher, owing its height to buildings constructed on mud brick platforms, and it was walled and thus physically separated from the Lower Town. It carries structures probably used for special public purposes, notably the warehouse and the Great Bath. The Lower Town is much larger but lower; it was also walled, contained the residential buildings, and shows the grid of streets and drains. Most Harappan settlements have a small high western part and a larger lower eastern section, but there are variations: at Dholavira and Lothal the entire settlement was fortified, and the Citadel at Lothal was not walled off but built at a height.

questions.q: Which architectural features of Mohenjodaro indicate planning?
answer: The division into Citadel and Lower Town; the mud brick platforms which restricted all building activity to a fixed area; the standardised brick ratio of four to two to one used at all Harappan settlements; the approximate grid of streets intersecting at right angles; the laying out of streets with drains before houses were built, requiring every house to have at least one wall along a street; and the uniform provision of bathrooms and house drains connected to the street drains.

questions.q: Are there other structures on the Citadel apart from the warehouse and the Great Bath?
answer: Yes. The plan of the Citadel shows, besides the warehouse and the Great Bath, a great courtyard, the structure marked as the college, a pillared hall, Main Street and Divinity Street, the stupa area, stairs, retaining walls including the eastern retaining wall, Jansen's excavated well, and the trenches of the early excavators.

questions.q: What are the modes of disposal of the dead prevalent at present? To what extent do these represent social differences?
answer: The chapter invites comparison with the Harappan practice, in which the dead were generally laid in pits, sometimes lined with bricks, occasionally with pottery, ornaments or copper mirrors, but on the whole without precious things. Against this it sets the massive pyramids of Egypt, some contemporaneous with the Harappan civilisation, many of them royal burials in which enormous quantities of wealth were buried — the clearest instance of burial marking social difference. Present-day modes of disposal should be assessed on the same test: the elaboration of the grave and the value of what is placed in it.

questions.q: Should the stone artefacts in the chapter be considered utilitarian objects or luxuries? Are there any that fall into both categories?
answer: Utilitarian objects are of daily use, made fairly easily out of ordinary materials such as stone or clay, and are usually found throughout settlements — the querns, stone blades and plain pottery belong here. Luxuries are rare, or made from costly non-local materials, or made with complicated technologies — the carnelian and steatite beads and the little faience pots belong here. Some objects fall into both categories: the chapter cites spindle whorls made of rare materials such as faience and asks explicitly whether these should be classified as utilitarian or as luxuries.

questions.q: What are some present-day methods used for long-distance exchange of goods? What are their advantages and problems?
answer: The chapter's point of comparison is the seal and sealing. A bag of goods had its mouth tied with rope, wet clay was affixed to the knot and one or more seals were pressed into it; if the sealing arrived intact, the consignment had not been tampered with, and the sealing also conveyed the identity of the sender. Present-day methods should be judged against these same two functions — guaranteeing that goods are untampered and authenticating the sender — together with the regulation of exchange, which the Harappans achieved through a precise system of chert weights and metal scale-pans.

questions.q: What were the possible routes from the Harappan region to Oman, Dilmun and Mesopotamia?
answer: Communication with Oman, Bahrain or Mesopotamia was likely by sea: Mesopotamian texts refer to Meluhha as a land of seafarers, and depictions of ships and boats are found on seals. Coastal routes and riverine routes along the Indus and its tributaries were probably used, while land routes were served by bullock carts, as terracotta toy models suggest. The coastal sites of Sutkagendor, Balakot, Nageshwar and Lothal lie along the plausible line of such a route.

questions.q: Could everybody in Harappan society have been equal?
answer: Some archaeologists are of the opinion that Harappan society had no rulers and that everybody enjoyed equal status, and the chapter observes that Harappan cemeteries show little social differentiation and that, on the whole, precious things were not buried with the dead. Against this stand the concentration of rare and valuable objects in Mohenjodaro and Harappa, their absence in small settlements such as Kalibangan, the recovery of all gold jewellery from hoards, and differences in the making of burial pits. The evidence therefore does not permit a firm answer either way.

questions.q: Which themes in this chapter would have interested Cunningham? Which issues have been of interest since 1947?
answer: Cunningham, the first Director-General of the ASI, preferred the written word — texts and inscriptions — and his main interest lay in the Early Historic period from about the sixth century BCE to the fourth century CE. He used the accounts of the Chinese Buddhist pilgrims, collected and translated inscriptions, and recovered artefacts of cultural value. He would therefore have been drawn to the seals and the script, but not to Harappa itself, which lay outside the pilgrims' itinerary and outside his framework.

Since 1947, with the major known sites falling within Pakistan, Indian archaeologists have located sites in India — a survey in Kutch, explorations in Punjab and Haryana, and the excavation of Kalibangan, Lothal, Rakhi Garhi and Dholavira. New issues have assumed importance: obtaining a cultural sequence, understanding the logic behind the location of sites, and determining the functions of artefacts. Since the 1980s there has been growing international interest, with modern scientific techniques including surface exploration, and archaeogenetic research began at Rakhigarhi in 2013.

questions.q: What aspects of the Harappan economy have been reconstructed from archaeological evidence?
answer: Subsistence, from charred grains, seeds and animal bones; agricultural technology, from plough models, the ploughed field at Kalibangan, canals at Shortughai and reservoirs at Dholavira; craft production, from raw material, tools, unfinished objects, rejects and waste at Chanhudaro, Lothal, Nageshwar, Balakot and Dholavira; procurement of raw materials, from the location of settlements and the identification of sources; exchange and long-distance trade, from seals and sealings, standardised chert weights, metal scale-pans, and Harappan objects found in Oman, Bahrain and Mesopotamia; and transport, from terracotta bullock carts and depictions of boats on seals. As the chapter concludes, decades of work have given us a fairly good idea of the Harappan economy, even while much about society, gender, literacy and religion remains speculative.
